content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In the broadest stream of Christian teaching, the moon is most commonly interpreted as the 'lesser light' that has no light of its own but reflects the light of the sun — symbolically, the Church (or the individual believer) reflecting the light of Christ, who is figured by the sun. This reading runs from patristic writers (e.g., Augustine, Ambrose, Origen) through medieval and modern devotional teaching. Bound up with this is the moon's role as a fixed, faithful witness in the heavens, a sign of God's ordered creation and covenant faithfulness.","primary_basis":["Genesis 1:14-18 (the greater and lesser lights; the moon rules the night)","Psalm 89:37 ('established forever like the moon, a faithful witness in the sky')","Psalm 136:9 ('the moon and stars to rule over the night')","Song of Solomon 6:10 ('fair as the moon,' traditionally applied to the Church or to Mary)","Revelation 12:1 (the woman with the moon under her feet, read as the Church or Mary)","Jeremiah 31:35-36 (the fixed order of moon and stars as guarantee of God's covenant)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Eschatological sign of judgment and the Day of the Lord: the darkening of the moon or its turning to blood signals cosmic upheaval and divine judgment. In terms of sheer frequency of biblical usage and preaching, this is arguably the most prominent use of the moon in Scripture itself.","basis":["Joel 2:31","Acts 2:20","Matthew 24:29 / Mark 13:24","Isaiah 13:10","Ezekiel 32:7","Revelation 6:12","Revelation 8:12"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Marker of appointed times, seasons, and festivals (new moons, the liturgical calendar), symbolizing God's ordering of sacred time — later read typologically as shadows fulfilled in Christ.","basis":["Genesis 1:14","Psalm 104:19","Numbers 28:11-14 (new moon offerings)","Isaiah 66:23","Colossians 2:16-17 (new moons as a shadow of things to come)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Marian symbolism in Catholic and Orthodox tradition: the moon under the woman's feet in Revelation 12 applied to the Virgin Mary; the moon's reflected light as an image of Mary reflecting Christ's glory (common within Catholic teaching, less so in Protestant interpretation).","basis":["Revelation 12:1","Song of Solomon 6:10 (traditional Marian application)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Mutability, changeableness, and instability: because the moon waxes and wanes, patristic and medieval writers used it as a figure of the changeable, mortal, sublunary world — or of the Church in its earthly, fluctuating condition as opposed to its heavenly glory.","basis":["Sirach 27:11 ('the fool changes like the moon' — deuterocanonical)","Genesis 1:16 (the 'lesser' light)","General patristic/medieval cosmological usage rather than a specific proof text"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Object of forbidden pagan worship: the moon as a symbol of idolatry and astral cults that Israel is warned against — a negative symbolic association.","basis":["Deuteronomy 4:19","Deuteronomy 17:3","2 Kings 23:5","Job 31:26-28","Jeremiah 8:2"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"In interpretations of Joseph's dream, the moon stands for a parent/matriarch (Rachel or Leah), giving a familial or 'Israel' referent to sun-moon-stars imagery; some interpreters extend this to read the moon in Revelation 12 as Israel/the patriarchal family.","basis":["Genesis 37:9-10","Revelation 12:1 (Israel-focused readings)"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"medium","notes":"The moon does not have one single settled symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation; instead there are several well-recognized strands. The 'reflected light / Church reflecting Christ' reading is the most distinctive and widely taught symbolic interpretation in the theological tradition, but the eschatological 'moon darkened / turned to blood' usage is more frequent in the biblical text itself and in preaching on prophecy. Which is 'primary' depends on whether one weights patristic-devotional tradition or biblical frequency; I have listed the traditional Church/reflection reading as primary while flagging the eschatological usage as a strong, common alternative. Confidence is medium precisely because the consensus is plural rather than singular."}
